e.t: Abelmaa is a proper name, also rendered “Avelmaa.” It identifies a specific named entity in the Greek Old Testament rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at 1 Kings 15:20. Because no surrounding verse text is provided here, the name’s particular significance in that passage cannot be described beyond its use as a proper name.

This LXX noun means “mistake”—something done or understood wrongly. It identifies an error as a thing that can be acknowledged, considered, or addressed. The word occurs four times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing once in Genesis and three times in the deuterocanonical books represented here. Its basic meaning remains focused on the mistake itself; the surrounding verse determines what was mistaken and what response is required.

This noun means “next of kin,” referring to a close family member who holds a recognized family connection or responsibility. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, in Ruth 4:1. The word’s basic sense identifies a person related closely enough to be regarded as family kin, rather than describing an emotion, action, or general association. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the responsibilities assigned to such a relative.

This verb means to offer a prize or offer rewards. It describes the act of presenting something as a reward, especially in connection with achievement or contest. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 17:12. The word focuses on the person or authority who provides the reward, rather than on the person who receives it. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Aithamin, also rendered Ethamin, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 18:17. The name itself does not provide a fuller meaning or definition; it identifies a particular named place or person in the biblical passage. Its precise referent must be understood from the surrounding text of Joshua, not from the name alone.

This Greek LXX noun means “enigma,” referring to something expressed in a puzzling, hidden, or difficult-to-understand way. It can describe a saying, question, or matter whose meaning is not immediately plain and calls for interpretation or discernment. The word occurs nine times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, including passages associated with Moses, the queen of Sheba, wisdom instruction, and Daniel. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the central idea remains a mysterious or puzzling expression.

Alae is a proper name, referring to a person named Alae in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, object, or spiritual principle, but a personal designation. The name occurs twice in the Greek text, both times in 2 Kings: once in 2 Kings 17:6 and again in 2 Kings 18:11. Since the available material provides no surrounding verse text or additional explanation of the person, the word itself is best understood simply as the name Alae.

Amasi is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, the name appears three times: in 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, and Nehemiah. The available English rendering preserves it as “Amasi.” Because no verse text or surrounding context is provided here, the name itself can be identified, while the particular person and role must be determined from each passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “dress”: to put clothing on someone or to clothe someone. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in 2 Kings and Job, so its attested use is limited. The surrounding verse determines who is being dressed and what emphasis the action carries. Its basic sense remains the act of supplying or putting on clothing.

This LXX Greek noun refers to the removal or destruction of something, especially its complete eradication or the carrying out of an execution. It presents an ending brought about by deliberate removal rather than merely a change or disappearance. The word occurs twice in the LXX corpus, in Judges and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central sense remains decisive elimination or execution.

This verb means “exchange”: to give one thing or position in return for another. It describes a reciprocal change, where something is offered and something else is received in its place. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Job and Proverbs. The exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains a substitution or trade between two parties or things.

This verb means “fall against; resist.” It describes opposing something rather than yielding to it. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs three times, in passages from Exodus and Numbers. Its central idea is to come against or stand against another person or thing. The precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the word consistently points to resistance or opposition rather than simple movement.

This noun means “abjuration” or “renunciation”—a formal rejection, disavowal, or turning away from something. It names the act rather than describing a person or action in progress. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 66:15, so its broader use cannot be established from repeated biblical examples. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea is a deliberate refusal or repudiation. The word is distinctively preserved in the Septuagint’s rendering of the Old Testament rather than being a Greek New Testament term.

This Greek LXX verb means “help” or “aid.” It describes giving assistance to someone or something in need, functioning as an action rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 4:16. The surrounding verse is needed to explain who is helped and why, but the word’s basic sense is straightforward: to provide active support or come to another’s assistance.

Asedōth, also rendered Asethoth, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an idea, action, or quality. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in Joshua 11:22. Because the available information identifies the name but does not include the verse text or surrounding context, its specific referent cannot be explained further here. The name should therefore be treated as a named entity whose significance is determined by its use in that passage.

Aspalathus is a noun naming a plant known by that name. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Sirach 24:15, and the translation preserves the plant name as “aspalathus.” The available lexical information does not identify its appearance, scent, medicinal use, or symbolic significance, so those details should not be added to its basic meaning. Its precise significance in Sirach 24:15 depends on the verse and surrounding passage.

This noun means “harshness” or “roughness,” describing a severe, hard, or unpleasant quality. It names the character of something rather than an action. In the Greek biblical corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 14:30. The available lexical meaning establishes its central sense, while the surrounding passage would be needed to determine exactly what or whom this quality describes in that verse.

This adjective describes someone or something as “unlying”—not characterized by falsehood or deceit. In ordinary Bible language, it points to what is truthful and dependable rather than deceptive. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Wisdom 7:17. Its precise force in that passage belongs to the surrounding wording, but its basic lexical sense is straightforward: it identifies what does not lie.

This is a proper name referring to Beersheba, also rendered in the gloss as “Virsavee.” It identifies a named place rather than describing an action, quality, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs twice, both times in Nehemiah: 11:27 and 11:30. Since no verse text is provided here, the word’s specific role in either sentence cannot be expanded beyond its function as a place-name.

“Gabaōthiarim” or “Gavaothiarim” is a proper name preserved as a distinct name in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as an ordinary action, quality, or object word, so its meaning is chiefly its identifying use rather than a general concept. It occurs once, in Joshua 18:28. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what the name identifies there.

Gedel, also rendered Yethil, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Ezra 2:56. The available wording identifies the person by name but does not provide an additional definition or explain the name’s origin. Its precise significance in that passage must therefore be understood from the surrounding verse and list of names, not from the name itself.

This noun means “weeping” or “wailing”—an outward expression of grief or sorrow. It describes audible mourning rather than a quiet inward feeling. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs four times, all in 3 Maccabees. One English rendering is “wailing,” which fits the word’s sense of vocal lament. The surrounding verse determines whose grief is being expressed and what caused it.

This Greek LXX verb means “multiply by ten.” It describes increasing something tenfold, rather than merely adding a small amount or making a general increase. The word appears once in the LXX corpus, in Baruch 4:28, so its normal meaning is clear from its explicit definition even though the surrounding verse text is not available here. As a verb, it expresses the action of bringing something to ten times its previous amount.

This Greek LXX verb describes someone or something as being in a particular condition or disposition. It can express how a person or thing is situated inwardly or otherwise arranged, rather than naming a specific action. In the Greek text of 3 Maccabees, it occurs twice, so its precise force in each sentence depends on the surrounding context. The related rendering “disposed” reflects this sense of being placed or inclined in a certain state.

This verb means “measure off”: to determine or mark the extent of something by measuring it. It describes a practical act of establishing dimensions or boundaries rather than merely looking at an object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 36 times, with most occurrences in Ezekiel, where measured spaces and boundaries are especially prominent. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on what is being measured, but its central idea remains the careful setting out of a measurable extent.

This verb means “cut to the quick; infuriated.” It describes a person being sharply affected inwardly, with the force of the word pointing to intense provocation rather than mild annoyance. As a verb, it expresses what happens to someone: they are driven into a state of deep agitation or anger. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 20:3. The exact nuance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb means “manage a house,” describing the work of directing, ordering, or caring for a household. It can therefore refer to responsible oversight rather than merely living in a house. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times: once in Daniel and four times in Wisdom. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is the active management of a household or its affairs.

This Greek LXX noun means a thicket—a dense, often tangled growth of trees or shrubs. It refers to a wooded or brush-covered place rather than to a person, action, or abstract idea. The word appears 63 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX material, showing that it is used for this ordinary landscape feature across many passages. Its precise significance in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

Eththi is a proper name identifying a person, rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 11 times across 10 verses, mainly in 2 Samuel and 1 Chronicles. The name itself carries no further meaning supplied here, so its significance comes from the surrounding passage whenever it appears. This LXX form should be understood as a personal name within the Greek Old Testament, not treated as a general Greek vocabulary term.

This verb means “expose; explain”: it describes making something known, open, or understandable. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it is used for the act of bringing information or a matter into clear view rather than keeping it hidden. The word occurs 12 times in this corpus, with many occurrences in Esther. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on what is being made known there.

This Greek LXX verb means “rub out; wipe out.” It describes removing something completely, whether by wiping it away or by bringing it to an end. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs 50 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, showing that this idea is used across a broad range of passages. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being removed and the surrounding sentence.

Eleada is a proper name, also rendered “Eleatha.” It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament (LXX), rather than describing an action, quality, or general concept. This name occurs once in the LXX, at 1 Chronicles 7:20. Because no verse text is supplied here, the name’s particular family and narrative setting should be read from that passage itself; the lexical evidence establishes the name, not a broader abstract meaning.

This Greek LXX adjective means “nine thousand,” describing a quantity of nine groups of one thousand. It functions as a number-word, identifying how many people or things are being counted rather than expressing an action, quality, or relationship. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both in 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning remains a precise numerical total: nine thousand.

Enos is a personal name, referring to a man named Enos rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, the name appears seven times across seven verses, chiefly in Genesis and once in 1 Chronicles. It is rendered consistently as “Enos,” preserving it as a name. The surrounding passages are needed to explain what is said about Enos in any particular verse.

This adjective describes something “wherein one feels joy” or is “delightsome.” It identifies a joyful or delightful quality rather than naming a person, action, or object by itself. In the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint), it occurs once, at Proverbs 11:3, so this is its only recorded use in that corpus. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the central idea remains something that brings delight or in which joy is felt.

Erchi, also rendered “Erkhi,” is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It does not describe an action, quality, or idea; it functions as a personal name. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, at 2 Samuel 23:35. Because the available information gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, its specific identity and role must be understood from that passage’s context.

This noun refers to ease or facility—the condition of being manageable or not difficult. It describes ease as a quality or circumstance rather than an action. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 2:25. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and paragraph, but its basic meaning is straightforward: something is approached or carried out with ease rather than difficulty.

Ephermem, also rendered Efermem, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Samuel 17:1. Because it is a name, its meaning is primarily identification: it distinguishes a particular person, place, or other named entity in the passage. The name itself does not provide enough information to determine which kind of entity it identifies without the surrounding verse text.

This Greek LXX verb means “unite” or “join.” It describes bringing people or things together rather than keeping them separate. As a verb, it expresses an action of joining or being joined. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 1:15. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains connection and union.

This word means “day,” referring to the ordinary period of daylight or to a defined day within the calendar. It is a noun used for time, dates, and periods marked by what happens during them. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 2,279 times, showing that it is a common way to identify a day or time period across the biblical narrative and laws. Its precise sense in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

Thakouath, also rendered Thakuath, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. Its meaning is therefore its identifying name, not a broader concept translated into English. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Chronicles 34:22. Without the verse text or surrounding passage, the name alone does not establish whether it refers to a person, place, or another named entity in that passage.

Iekemia is a personal name, functioning as a proper noun rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at 1 Chronicles 3:18. Since the available information identifies the word only as the name “Iekemia,” its meaning is best understood as the designation of a particular individual, while the surrounding verse supplies the details about that person.

Iessai, also rendered Iesse, is a proper name—the personal name of an individual rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the LXX corpus, it appears 38 times, beginning in Ruth and continuing through later historical and wisdom books. Its precise reference is determined by the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is simply the person’s name.

This word means “Judean.” As a noun, it identifies a Judean person; as an adjective, it describes something connected with Judeans. It is used throughout the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical writings, appearing 197 times in this LXX corpus. The word therefore marks a person or thing by Judean identity, while the surrounding verse determines what is being said about that person or thing.

This word is the personal name “Jonathan,” also rendered “Ionathan.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 214 times, showing that it is used as a recurring proper name across these writings. Its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the person and surrounding passage being discussed.

This word means “seat”: a place or object used for sitting. It is a noun describing a seat in ordinary, concrete terms, rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 16 times, so its meaning is consistent across a range of passages. The exact significance of a particular seat depends on the surrounding verse, but the word itself points to the seat.

This Greek LXX noun means a “basket with pointed bottom.” It refers to a particular kind of container, rather than to a general basket in every possible sense. The word appears five times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, including passages in Deuteronomy, 2 Kings, Jeremiah, and Sirach. Its exact significance in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains a distinctive basket shaped with a pointed base.

This verb means to deem someone or something worthy—that is, to judge it suitable for a certain honor, privilege, treatment, or action. It expresses an assessment of worth rather than merely noticing or naming something. The word occurs four times in this Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees, 3 Maccabees, and 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in any one verse depends on what the surrounding sentence says is being considered worthy.

This Greek LXX verb means “lie; laid,” describing something resting in a position or being placed there. It can refer to the state of lying somewhere, or to something that has been laid down. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs 21 times, so its central sense is a straightforward description of position or placement rather than an abstract idea. Its exact force in a passage depends on the surrounding wording.

This Greek LXX verb means “exhort” or “command”: it describes urging someone to act or giving an authoritative order. Its basic force is active and directive, whether the instruction is presented as strong encouragement or as a command that expects obedience. It occurs 23 times across the Greek LXX corpus, including books such as 1–4 Maccabees and Bel and the Dragon. The precise force in any verse depends on who is speaking, who receives the instruction, and the surrounding words.

This word means “little girl.” It is a noun used to refer to a young female child in the Greek Old Testament. Its basic sense identifies the person being spoken of, while the surrounding sentence determines what is being said about her. The word occurs 18 times across 17 verses in the LXX, including passages in Ruth, 1 Samuel, and Esther. [p03:word:lxx:L707832:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L707832:occurrences]

This word means “flesh-hook,” a hooked utensil used for handling pieces of meat. It is a noun naming a physical tool rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears nine times across nine verses, including descriptions of furnishings and utensils associated with worship and accounts involving the handling of sacrificial meat. The word’s basic meaning remains practical and specific: a hook designed to grasp or move flesh. Its precise significance in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Kōrē, also rendered Kori, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a particular person or family name in passages from Chronicles. It occurs three times, in 1 Chronicles and 2 Chronicles. The available meaning information gives the name itself but does not provide a further definition or explanation of its origin. Its precise identification in each passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This verb means “pay,” describing the act of giving what is owed or required. It is a Greek LXX word used three times, all in Sirach, so its basic sense is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not provided here. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. Its precise force in each passage depends on what is being paid and the surrounding context. The word occurs in Sirach 20:10, Sirach 20:14, and Sirach 29:11.

Marisa is a proper name used to identify a person in the Greek Old Testament and Greek deuterocanonical text. It is not presented here as a descriptive word with an expressed meaning beyond the name itself. In this LXX corpus, Marisa occurs four times across three verses: twice in 1 Chronicles, once in 2 Chronicles, and once in 2 Maccabees. The name is rendered “Marisa” where an English rendering is available. The particular person identified depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

Massōch, also given as Massokh, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Joshua 11:8. The available information identifies the name itself but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain whether it refers to a person, place, or people group in that passage. Its meaning is therefore best stated as the proper name “Massōch; Massokh,” with its precise referent determined by the context of Joshua 11:8.

Mesopotamia is a proper name for a region. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies the land associated with several ancestral journeys and family connections, especially in Genesis. The word occurs 17 times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing most often in Genesis, and it is rendered “Mesopotamia.” As a place-name, it points to a geographic region rather than describing a person, action, or quality. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and the people or journeys being discussed.

This noun means “hatred of guests”—a hostile rejection of people who should receive welcome or hospitality. It names an attitude toward guests rather than an action performed by them. In the Greek LXX material, it occurs once, in Wisdom 19:13. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but the word itself clearly describes opposition or hostility toward guests. The meaning is therefore negative: not merely failing to welcome visitors, but holding animosity toward them.

The word means “mulberry,” referring to the fruit of the mulberry tree. It is a concrete noun naming an ordinary plant food rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 6:34. That reference identifies where the word appears, while its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. Its clear lexical sense is the fruit itself.

This noun refers to a Nazarite—a person consecrated by Nazarite vows. It identifies someone set apart to God through a specific vow of dedication, rather than describing an ordinary personal name or general religious feeling. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, the word occurs twice, including once in Lamentations and once in 1 Maccabees. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central meaning remains a person marked by consecration through Nazarite vows.

This adjective means “youthful,” describing someone or something associated with youth or the qualities of being young. It identifies a characteristic rather than naming a person or action. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 4:8. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning remains a description of youthfulness. [p03:word:lxx:L709290:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L709290:occurrences]

This word means “polished,” describing something made smooth, finished, or given a refined surface. It functions as an adjective and can also serve as a noun, identifying something with that quality. In the LXX corpus, it occurs three times: twice in Old Testament books and once in Sirach. Its appearances are in 1 Chronicles 22:2, Amos 5:11, and Sirach 22:17, though the surrounding verse text is needed to explain its particular force in each passage.

This verb means to acknowledge something as true or to agree with it. It describes a person openly admitting, recognizing, or accepting a matter rather than denying it. The same basic idea can also express agreement with what another person has said or declared. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs nine times, showing a recurring word for acknowledgment or agreement across these books.

Ooliba is a proper name referring to a woman named in the Greek Old Testament. The name is also rendered Ooliva. It occurs six times in the Septuagint, all within five verses of Ezekiel 23, from Ezekiel 23:4 through Ezekiel 23:44. As a personal name, it identifies the same named figure whenever it appears; the particular significance of that figure in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “when” or “once”. It is an adverb that marks the time or circumstance in which something happens. It can introduce an event that is expected, repeated, or dependent on another action, helping connect one statement with what follows. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 185 times, showing that it is a regular way to express timing across many kinds of passages. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This noun means “seaboard” or “seashore,” referring to land along the edge of the sea. It identifies a coastal region or shoreline rather than the sea itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 9:1, so its precise reference there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word’s basic idea remains a geographical one: the shore or coastal area bordering the sea.

Patachron is a noun preserved as “patachron,” but its precise English meaning is not identified here. It appears twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in Isaiah. Without an English gloss, verse text, or surrounding context, it would be unsafe to assign it a broader meaning or describe the thing it names. The term occurs in Isaiah 8:21 and Isaiah 37:38, but those references alone do not establish its lexical sense.

This verb means “put around/on.” It describes placing something onto or around another person or thing, such as clothing, an ornament, or another covering. Its basic sense is an action of putting something in position rather than merely possessing it. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 49 times, showing that this action is used in a range of ordinary and ceremonial settings. The precise force in any passage depends on what is being placed and what receives it.

This noun means “wanderer”—someone who moves from place to place rather than remaining settled. It presents a person by the characteristic of wandering, and its basic meaning is concise and direct. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Hosea 9:17. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its normal lexical sense is a person who wanders.

This word means “ambassador”: a person sent to represent a ruler, government, or community in dealings with others. It is a noun describing someone who carries an official message or acts on behalf of those who sent him. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs six times, including five times in 1 Maccabees and once in 2 Chronicles. The word therefore refers to an appointed representative, not merely any messenger, though the surrounding passage determines the specific mission involved.

This LXX verb means to “expect” or “suppose”—to look for something as likely, or to regard something as a possibility. It describes an act of anticipation or judgment rather than a person, object, or place. The word occurs 12 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, including passages from Deuteronomy, Psalms, Lamentations, Wisdom, and the Maccabean books. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on what the surrounding sentence says.

This verb means to call someone or something by a name. It describes the act of giving or using a name when referring to a person, place, or thing. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 6:2. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly who or what is being named there, but the word itself centers on naming or calling by name.

gl: light and keep up a fire; watch a fire
d: light and keep up a fire; watch a fire

e.t: This verb means “light and keep up a fire; watch a fire.” It describes an active task involving starting a fire, maintaining its flame, or keeping watch over it. The word functions as a verb, so it expresses something a person does rather than naming an object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 7:4. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, since the verse text is not available here.

Rammath is a proper name preserved as “Rammath” or “Rhammath” in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a descriptive word that explains an action or quality; it identifies a particular named entity in the text. This LXX word occurs once, in 2 Kings 9:16, so its specific referent must be understood from that passage rather than from the name alone.

This Greek noun means “flow of water” or “current,” referring to water moving along or through a channel. It names a physical stream or movement of water rather than an action, feeling, or abstract idea. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 4:26. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense remains a flowing movement of water. [p03:word:lxx:L711299:identity; p03:word:lxx:L711299:occurrences; p01:word:lxx:L711299:reference:0]

Samalai, also rendered Samale, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Ezra 2:46, identifying a named individual in that passage. The name itself does not communicate a broader idea or spiritual quality; its function is to designate someone. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain that person’s specific role or place in the passage.

Sarou, also written Saru, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezra 10:40. The available wording identifies the person by name but does not provide a broader definition or explain the name’s origin. Its significance in that passage must therefore be understood from the surrounding verse and account, rather than from the name itself.

Siona is a proper name rendered from the Greek Old Testament, referring to a named person, place, or other specific designation rather than expressing a general quality or action. Its precise referent is not identified by the available word-level information. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Joshua 19:19. The English rendering preserves the name as “Siona,” rather than translating it into an ordinary descriptive word.

This adverb means “diligently,” describing action carried out with careful effort, seriousness, and earnest attention. It tells how something is done rather than naming a person, object, or event. In the Greek of the Septuagint, it appears once, in Wisdom 2:6. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding words, but its basic sense is to act earnestly and with purposeful care.

This LXX Greek noun means “composition; concert,” referring to an arrangement or joining together. It can describe something formed by bringing parts into an ordered whole, or an agreement among persons or things. The word occurs 12 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, including several occurrences in Daniel 5. Its precise force in any passage depends on how the surrounding sentence uses the idea of composition or concert.

This noun means “coming together; meeting,” describing people or things joining or converging. It can refer to an actual meeting or to parts that come together as one arrangement. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 10 times, with many occurrences in Exodus describing the joining of parts of the tabernacle and priestly clothing. The central idea is connection through coming together, whether referring to people meeting or components fitting together.

This noun means “connection”: something that joins, links, or holds things together. In the Greek Old Testament, it describes a binding link rather than an isolated thing. The word occurs eight times across seven verses, including passages in Kings, Job, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being joined and the surrounding context.
